question: to the Commission Markéta Gregorová (Verts/ALE), Leila Chaibi (The Left), David Cormand (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The media organisation Disclose has revealed that French police officers were equipped with ‘NEO’ mobile phones containing software that allows for real-time biometric identification. The software can be used for investigations related to crimes, offences and even certain minor offences. The facial recognition feature does not seem to have had any safeguards in place regarding its use: police officers have used the software for mere identity checks. The software connects directly to the ‘TAJ’ database, which is estimated to contain 17 million files regarding suspects and 48 million files regarding victims, with an estimated 9 million facial images1. The database can contain very sensitive information, such as religion, sexual orientation, union membership, etc. The TAJ database has been heavily criticised by the French Data Protection Authority for its lack of accuracy2. 1.

Does the Commission consider the system as being a real-time remote biometric identification system and does it consider that the system complies with the temporal, geographic and personal limitations established under the AI Act?
Does the Commission consider the requirement for prior judicial or independent administrative authorisation to be met?
Does the Commission consider the crimes and offences covered to be compliant with Annex II to the AI Act?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) Under the AI Act1, the use of real-time remote biometric identification (RBI) systems in publicly accessible spaces for the purposes of law enforcement is prohibited, unless and in so far as such use is strictly necessary for one of the three objectives specified under Article 5(1)(h) of the AI Act and the Member State law permitting the use of such systems comply with the requirements in Article 5(2)-(7) of the AI Act. The following three objectives are listed in Article 5(1)(h): (i) the targeted search for victims of three specific serious crimes and missing persons, (ii) the prevention of imminent threats to life or physical safety or a genuine threat of terrorist attacks, and (iii) the localisation or identification of suspects and offenders of certain serious crimes as listed in Annex II. According to the requirements in Article 5(2)-(7) of the AI Act, the deployment of a real-time RBI system in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes shall be subject to a prior authorisation granted by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding. The prohibition in Article 5(1)(h) of the AI Act started to apply as from 2 February 2025. However, the provisions on the enforcement of the AI Act will only start to apply on 2 August 2026. Therefore, the enforcement of Article 5 of the AI Act cannot be initiated earlier at either national or EU level. The Commission will observe this matter closely.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence,
